questions.q:
A spinner can land on red, blue, green or yellow. The table shows the probabilities.

Colour        Red    Blue   Green   Yellow
Probability   0.35   0.2     x       2x

Find the probability that the spinner lands on yellow.
questions.tip: Probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1.

questions.q:
Two fair four-sided spinners, each numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, are spun and the scores are added.
Find the probability that the total is 5.
ms: M1: 16 equally likely outcomes, with 4 giving a total of 5 ((1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1))
questions.model:
There are 4 × 4 = 16 equally likely outcomes. A total of 5 comes from (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2) and (4, 1): 4 outcomes.
P(total = 5) = 4/16 = 1/4.
questions.tip: A sample space diagram (4 by 4 grid) makes it easy to count the outcomes.

questions.q:
A bag contains 5 red counters and 3 blue counters. Two counters are taken at random, without replacement.
(a) Find the probability that both counters are red. [2]
(b) Find the probability that the counters are different colours. [2]
(c) Find the probability that at least one counter is blue. [1]
questions.tip: Without replacement, the second-pick denominators drop to 7.

questions.q:
In a class of 60 students, 32 play football (F), 25 play tennis (T) and 10 play both.
(a) Draw a Venn diagram to show this information, giving the number in each region. [2]
A student is chosen at random.
(b) Find the probability that the student plays neither sport. [1]
(c) Given that the student plays tennis, find the probability that the student also plays football. [2]
ms: B1: F only 22, both 10, T only 15
questions.model:
(a) Football only = 32 − 10 = 22; both = 10; tennis only = 25 − 10 = 15; neither = 60 − 22 − 10 − 15 = 13.
(b) P(neither) = 13/60.
(c) P(F | T) = 10 ÷ 25 = 2/5.
questions.tip: Fill in the intersection first, then subtract it from each total.

questions.q:
In a factory, 2% of items made are faulty. An inspector checks every item.
The inspector rejects 95% of faulty items. The inspector also rejects 10% of items that are not faulty.
(a) Draw a tree diagram to show this information. [2]
(b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen item is rejected. [2]
(c) Given that an item is rejected, find the probability that it is faulty. [2]
(d) Comment on how well the inspection works. [1]
ms: B1: first branches faulty 0.02, not faulty 0.98
B1: second branches rejected 0.95 / accepted 0.05 after faulty, and rejected 0.1 / accepted 0.9 after not faulty
(d) B1: e.g. most rejected items (about 84%) are not actually faulty, so many good items are wasted / the inspection should be improved (ft)
questions.model:
(a) First branches: faulty 0.02, not faulty 0.98. After faulty: rejected 0.95, accepted 0.05. After not faulty: rejected 0.1, accepted 0.9.
(b) P(rejected) = 0.02 × 0.95 + 0.98 × 0.1 = 0.019 + 0.098 = 0.117.
(c) P(faulty | rejected) = 0.019 ÷ 0.117 = 0.162.
(d) Only about 16% of rejected items are actually faulty, so the inspector rejects many good items. This is wasteful, so the inspection method should be improved.
questions.tip: For 'given that', divide by the probability of the condition you are given (here P(rejected)).

questions.q:
200 people were asked whether they use a gym.

               Uses a gym   Does not use a gym   Total
Under 30           54              66             120
30 and over        26              54              80
Total              80             120             200

A person is chosen at random. G is the event 'uses a gym' and U is the event 'is under 30'.
(a) Find P(G ∪ U). [2]
(b) Determine whether the events G and U are independent. Show your working. [3]
(c) Find P(U | G). [2]
questions.tip: To test independence, compare P(A ∩ B) with P(A) × P(B) and write a conclusion.
